screenconnect-cleanup.html:
ScreenConnect Cleanup

Designed by pupontech in collaboration with Rubin IT. A read-only mirror of this repository is kept at RubinITCompTelecom/screenconnect-cleanup. Make changes in pupontech/screenconnect-cleanup.

BETA: 1.8.13-beta.2. Download the Latest beta release. Includes the end-to-end review fixes, the reviewed cleanup repairs, persistence selection checkboxes, staged KVRT in Offline mode, clear Online continuation choices and preserved Online attempts. Live elevated Windows acceptance is still required. Existing releases remain available; the installer command below downloads GitHub's Latest release.

A Windows technician tool for PCs where a scammer got remote access through ScreenConnect. It usually gets there from an invite email the user clicked (a fake invoice, meeting or "document shared with you"), which installs ScreenConnect connected to the scammer's server.

Antivirus will not catch it. ScreenConnect is a legitimate, signed program that IT companies use every day, so no AV treats it as a virus. This tool finds every ScreenConnect instance, shows which relay server each one calls home to (the only reliable way to tell the scammer's copy from the customer's own IT), removes the ones you choose, checks what else was left behind to start up with Windows, runs the AV scanners for any other malware, and writes a report.

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pupontech/screenconnect-cleanup/main/install-latest.ps1 | iex

Read install-latest.ps1 first if you prefer; it only downloads, verifies, extracts and launches. Running it again with the same version just opens the existing copy.

Needs: Windows 10 or 11, an administrator account (the launcher asks once through UAC), PowerShell 5.1 (built in). Internet only for the Online half and Stage tools.

Using the window

Double-click START-HERE-GUI.bat, approve the administrator prompt, pick what to run and press Start.

Choice Internet What it does
Offline not needed Preflight, before snapshot, detection, removal of the ScreenConnect you choose, optional staged KVRT scan, persistence review, optional power-options repair, after snapshot + diff, local report. Missing KVRT is skipped. ESET and Malwarebytes run in Online mode. Downloads and uploads nothing.
Online needed Downloads and runs KVRT, ESET Online Scanner and Malwarebytes, checks startup items again after the scans, optional AV uninstall, shares the report if the box is ticked. Continues this PC's last Offline run if there is one; otherwise offers cleanup first or scanners only.
Detect only not needed Preflight, snapshot, detection and the report. Changes nothing. Use it to look before you decide.
Stage tools needed Downloads the scanners into the tool folder for later. Changes nothing on the PC.

The left column shows every step and its state (done, skipped and why, failed). The console at the bottom shows the scripts' own output live. Open log opens the full log; Open RIT-SCC folder (top right) opens C:\RIT-SCC, where every run is kept.

During this tool's snapshots, remote-access detection and persistence inventory, Stop scan cancels the tool scan and ends the run before later steps. Evidence is kept and the interrupted scan is marked cancelled. Pause after scan lets the current scan finish, then waits for Resume before the next step. These controls are unavailable once cleanup is approved. The external antivirus programs keep their own controls.

When it finishes you see each ScreenConnect instance as a card. The relay host is the line that matters: a host you do not recognise is the scammer's.

The usual job

  1. Take the PC off the network (unplug the cable, turn Wi-Fi off) if a session might still be live.

  2. Run Offline. For each ScreenConnect instance choose Remove (the default) or Keep (for example the customer's own support agent). Type REMOVE to confirm; the button stays disabled until you do.

  3. When asked to open the review windows, say Yes and go through them (see below).

  4. Read the report. It opens by itself and a copy is left on the Desktop.

  5. Reconnect and run Online. Say yes to continuing the offline run; run the scanners you want. If Share the sanitized report is ticked (it is by default), the report is shared at the end and the link appears in the window and in the report. Untick it and nothing is uploaded.

A PC that must stay offline: run only Offline. Everything stays in C:\RIT-SCC\<PC>-<id>\ and nothing is shared.

The review windows: go through them

Removing ScreenConnect is not always the end of it. Once a scammer is on a PC they often leave a way back in: a scheduled task, a service, a Run key or a file in a startup folder that reinstalls the remote tool or runs something else at every boot. The tool scans for these, but its matches are guesses, and the most dangerous kinds (services, WMI subscriptions, hidden tasks, Winlogon settings) are only reported, never removed automatically, because removing the wrong one can break Windows. That part needs a person.

So near the end of the Offline run the tool offers to open, side by side:

  • Services and Task Scheduler
  • the scheduled-task folder on disk and every startup folder it looked at
  • the run's evidence folder (with the exported task definitions) and the quarantine folder

It also prints a list of everything it flagged: what it is, the command it runs, why it was flagged, where to find it, and whether it is review-only. Opening the windows changes nothing.

What to look for: anything installed or created around the time of the incident, anything that runs from a user's AppData or Temp folder, another remote-access tool (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, RustDesk...), or a name you do not recognise. Compare with the flagged list. Startup items the tool can remove are removed only when you select them and type REMOVE; services and the rest you deal with by hand.

What you get

Every run has its own folder, C:\RIT-SCC\<PC>-<id>\ (locked to administrators, so nothing running as the user can tamper with it between the two halves):

File / folder What it is
report.html The investigation report (also copied to the Desktop). Instances, relay hosts, install dates, startup items found, before/after diff, scanner results, a credential-reset checklist.
report-after-scans.html Online half: the report rebuilt after the scanners. This is the one that is shared.
connectwise-report.zip Sanitized package (report JSON, technician summary, manifest) for the ConnectWise Trust Center. Never sent automatically.
quarantine\..., removal-manifest.json Everything removed, moved here, never deleted, with original path and hash.
detect\, snapshots, logs\ Raw evidence, before/after snapshots and every step's log.

Sharing (your choice). The Online choice has a tick box, Share the sanitized report, ticked by default. Ticked: the report is posted to the MicroBin server in files\microbin-url.txt (read-only, deleted after one week) and the link goes at the top of the report. Unticked: nothing is uploaded and everything stays on this PC. The Offline half and Detect only never upload anything.

What is shared: ScreenConnect relay hosts, instance IDs and thumbprints, file names and hashes, install dates and an anonymous PC ID (a short hash, not the computer name). Nothing personal is sent: no computer name, user or account names, network address of the PC, raw config, evidence, credentials or keys, and user folder names are replaced by <USERPROFILE>. The copy on this PC (connectwise-report.zip and report.html) keeps the full details.

Sharing is not a report to ConnectWise. It gives your team one link with what ConnectWise needs (the relay host and instance ID) to shut down the scammer's server; you file that report yourself.

Why relay host, and what it does not do

Signature, publisher and file hash are the same whether ScreenConnect belongs to the customer's IT or to the scammer. What differs is the relay server each instance is configured to call, so the tool reads that from every instance and puts it first.

  • The scanners are for the other malware that came along. They do not replace the ScreenConnect step.
  • Removing the agent does not undo the access. Passwords, browser sessions, mail rules and new accounts may be compromised; the report ends with a credential-reset checklist for that reason.
  • Other remote tools (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, RustDesk and 11 more) are detected and listed, not removed. Turn them on in files\targets.json.

Console launchers

Everything in the window is also available without it, in files\:

Launcher Same as
START-HERE-OFFLINE.bat Offline (steps 1-7). Asks Keep any ScreenConnect? [y/N], then one typed y.
START-HERE-ONLINE.bat Online (steps 1-5).
START-HERE.bat The original full run in one go (1-9); --stage = Stage tools.
Run-DetectRemoteAccess.bat Detection only, results to Desktop\RemoteAccessScan\.

Use them if the window will not open on a PC. How the two halves hand over and how they differ from the full run: OFFLINE-ONLINE-SPLIT.md.

remote-access-tool-blocker.html:
vibe coded use at your own risk

Remote-access tool blocker (Windows App Control + optional ESET list)

Designed by pupontech in collaboration with Rubin IT. A read-only mirror of this repository is kept at RubinITCompTelecom/remote-access-tool-blocker. Make changes in pupontech/remote-access-tool-blocker.

Blocks the legitimate remote-support tools that tech-support scammers abuse — AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, RustDesk, UltraViewer, Supremo, AeroAdmin and around fifty more — on ordinary Windows 10/11 PCs.

Most home and small-business PCs run consumer antivirus, so this is built to work on a stock PC with nothing but Windows on it. The blocking is done by Windows App Control (WDAC) deny rules built from each vendor's code-signing certificate, so it catches the program wherever it is: renamed, saved from an email attachment, sitting in Downloads, or run from a USB stick.

An optional second layer adds the tools' websites (download pages and web consoles) to ESET's web filter.

What it does

There are three independent protection layers. Use whichever fit the PC you are working on.

Layer What it blocks How it is applied How to undo
Windows App Control (WDAC) deny policy — program 1 The programs, wherever they are — renamed, email attachment, Downloads, USB Fully scripted Scripted (+ restart)
ESET web filter ("List of blocked addresses") — program 2 The tools' websites — download pages and web consoles Generated list, pasted by hand into ESET By hand in ESET
ESET "potentially unsafe applications" Known remote tools, flagged by ESET itself One manual toggle Toggle off

The App Control layer is the load-bearing one. The ESET layers are optional extras for PCs that run ESET.

Quick start

The full kit is two separate programs, in two folders:

Folder Program What it does Needs
1\ START-HERE.bat Blocks the remote-access programs (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect …) with Windows App Control Administrator. No antivirus.
2\ START-HERE.bat Builds the list of the tools' websites and opens ESET + the paste guide ESET installed. No admin needed.

They are independent — run either one, or both. Neither needs the other.

  1. Download the release ZIP you want:
    • remote-tools-block-windows-<version>.zip — the program blocker only. No antivirus needed. Start here.
    • full-kit-eset-<version>.zip — both programs, as folders 1 and 2.
  2. Extract it anywhere on the PC. Keep the folders together — the launchers find the scripts relative to themselves.
  3. Program 1: open folder 1, double-click START-HERE.bat and accept the administrator prompt.
  4. TeamViewer / AnyDesk / Splashtop / RustDesk start unticked (allowed) on a fresh PC. Ticked = blocked. An existing program policy still loads its installed choices.
  5. Press BLOCK.
  6. Program 2 (only if the PC runs ESET): open folder 2, double-click START-HERE.bat, press BUILD, then import the file into ESET BY HAND — the program cannot do it and cannot verify it. See The ESET paste.

When program 1 applies the block it also copies a standalone undo tool to C:\RemoteAccessToolBlocker on that PC — see Undoing it later. It is there so the block can be reverted later without the original kit, the network, or this repository.

To undo immediately: program 1 → press UNDO, then restart the PC. Program 2 → take the website list back out of ESET by hand, following the guide.

The status line always shows the current state — PROTECTED, TEST MODE or NOT protected — and what each toggle is set to. Refresh status lists recent events: [3077] means a program was blocked, [3076] means one would have been blocked (audit mode).

The ESET paste — MUST BE DONE BY HAND BY A TECHNICIAN

⚠️ THIS STEP CANNOT BE AUTOMATED. A TECHNICIAN MUST DO IT BY HAND.

The BLOCK button does everything else itself. It cannot add the website list to ESET: ESET's URL list is a GUI import/paste with no scriptable interface, and this project deliberately does not guess at ESET's configuration XML. A technician must import the file into ESET by hand, following the steps below.

Do not skip this step and do not assume it happened. Until it is done, the ESET website layer of the block is not active — the programs are still blocked by Windows App Control, but the tools' download sites and web consoles are not.

Program 2 BUILD writes one combined file, eset-blocked-urls.txt, opens its folder with the file selected, opens the list itself in Notepad alongside the instructions, and copies the full file path to the clipboard (not the list contents). The path is also printed in the window. Open the list folder reopens it without rebuilding.

Both programs start with TeamViewer, AnyDesk, Splashtop and RustDesk unticked (allowed). Their checkboxes are independent. Program 1 loads installed choices when an existing policy is detected.

Review before import: the combined list now includes previously optional AV-update, SaaS and VPN domains. Review optional-tier rows in url-review.csv and remove services the client needs from the import file. The protected-root and allow-domain safety filters remain active. There is no second optional import file.

  1. In ESET, press F5 -> Protections -> Web access protection -> URL list management -> Address list / Edit.
  2. Add a new list of type Blocked, named RMM scam block (lolrmm), with List active ticked.
  3. Inside it choose Import. Paste the copied file path into File name, then Open. If clipboard copy failed, browse to the file in the folder that opened. Do not paste the path into Enter multiple values.
  4. Click OK on every window to save.
  5. Test a website that actually appears in the generated file. AnyDesk is allowed by default, so it is not a valid default test.

To undo, remove this named list or untick List active. Do not remove unrelated pre-existing entries. Program 2 does not apply the Windows program block or verify ESET import; use program 1 independently.

See docs/eset-import-guide.md and the guide that opens in Notepad.

Undoing it later

Program 1 installs the undo tool to C:\RemoteAccessToolBlocker on the PC when it applies the block, so the block can be removed later without the original kit, the network, or this repository. It installs the ESET-free variant — program 1 blocks only programs, so it must never hand out ESET removal steps.

C:\RemoteAccessToolBlocker\
  Run-Revert.bat                          <- double-click this
  Revert-RemoteAccessBlock-WinOnly.ps1    (App Control removal only, ESET-free)
  README.txt
  policy\                                 (the built policies, so it can put the block back)
  backups\                                (created by the first revert)

Program 2 installs the ESET-aware variant to the same folder when it builds a list — that is what adds the ESET removal steps and the guide:

C:\RemoteAccessToolBlocker\
  Revert-RemoteAccessBlock.ps1            (also handles the ESET website list)
  docs\eset-remove-guide.txt
  README.txt

Whichever program ran last owns the variant: program 2 removes the ESET-free copy when it installs the full one, so exactly one variant is ever present and the tool always matches what was actually blocked on the PC. A PC that only ever ran program 1 therefore never sees an ESET step.

Because that folder is a permanent, scriptable tool sitting on the machine, note what it is: it lets anyone with local administrator rights undo the block. That is deliberate — the alternative is a PC you cannot un-block without hunting down the original kit.

Two variants, matching what actually ran on the PC

The variant installed is chosen by which program put it there, because a PC that only ran program 1 (or the Windows-only kit) has no ESET layer and must never be told to go un-block something that was never blocked:

Program used Variant installed Behaviour
Program 1 (and the Windows-only kit) Revert-RemoteAccessBlock-WinOnly.v*.ps1 App Control removal only. Never touches ESET — no ESET window, no ESET steps, no guide, and it does not even read the LOLRMM-UrlList folder.
Program 2 (the website list) Revert-RemoteAccessBlock.v*.ps1 Removes the policy and walks you through taking the website list back out of ESET.

Program 2 removes the ESET-free variant when it installs the full one, so exactly one variant is ever present and it always matches what was blocked. Both variants are generated from one source, so they cannot drift.

Command What it does
Run-Revert.bat Undo the block. Backs up first, then removes the policy (and opens the ESET guide on the full variant).
Run-Revert.bat -WhatIf Dry run — shows every step and changes nothing.
Run-Revert.bat -Restore Put a previously backed-up block back, with its original toggles.
Run-Revert.bat -NoPause Don't wait for a key press at the end (remote/unattended use).
Run-Revert.bat -RemoveFolder After reverting, also delete the folder and its backups.

Revert never destroys the ability to restore. Before it removes anything it copies the installed policy, its toggles and mode, the generated ESET lists (full variant only) and a machine summary into backups\<timestamp>\, one dated folder per revert, never overwritten. -Restore reads those back.

On the full variant, the ESET website list is the one part it cannot do for you. ESET's URL list is a UI import/paste with no scriptable interface, so the tool backs up the generated list, opens ESET, opens docs\eset-remove-guide.txt, and tells you exactly what to click. If you pasted into ESET's own built-in list rather than a list you created, the guide warns you to check it was empty beforehand — that removal is not undoable from ESET's side.

-WhatIf is the safe way to see what a revert would do on a live machine.

Test before you enforce

Press Test mode first. It installs the same policy in audit mode: nothing is blocked, but Windows logs what would have been. Run the program you expect to be blocked, then Refresh status and confirm you see a 3076 for it. Only then press BLOCK.

What gets blocked

Always on — around 55 tools from 52 vendors are covered, including ScreenConnect (ConnectWise Control), UltraViewer, Supremo, AeroAdmin, Remote Utilities, Remote Manipulator System, Lite Manager, DW Service, Tactical RMM, Atera, NinjaRMM, Action1, Syncro, SuperOps, MeshCentral, HopToDesk, Getscreen, SimpleHelp, ISL Online and more. The full list of rules is in policy/signers.csv.

Switchable per PC — four tools are on toggles, because a client may legitimately use one:

Toggle Tool Default
T TeamViewer blocked
A AnyDesk blocked
S Splashtop allowed
R RustDesk blocked

Splashtop is allowed by default because it is commonly used by IT shops as their own support tool. Blocking it cuts off that shop's access to the PC, so the window warns before you do it. Change this default for your own deployment — see Configuration.

All 16 toggle combinations are pre-built as .cip files in policy/variants/, so a PC that cannot build policies (a Windows Home PC, or any PC without the ConfigCI tooling) can still switch between them.

Optional vendors, not blocked by default — the vendor list is deliberately hand-checked. Several remote-access vendors also sign software that people use on purpose (NetSupport School, Impero/Netop and Veyon in schools; GoTo, Zoho, AOMEI, RealVNC, Famatech/Advanced IP Scanner, Kaseya, N-able, Ivanti), so they are excluded unless you ask for them with -IncludeOptional when rebuilding.

Never blocked — a hard guard rejects well-known publishers regardless of the lists: Microsoft, Google, ESET, Adobe and similar. This exists because the upstream catalogue attaches unrelated certificates to some tools; an unattended rebuild against it would otherwise block ordinary software.

How it works

The policy starts from Microsoft's own AllowAll.xml template — allow-everything — and adds deny rules for specific code-signing certificates in the user-mode signing scenario only. Script enforcement is left off, so PowerShell is not forced into Constrained Language Mode and normal administration keeps working.

For each vendor certificate there are two rules:

  • a leaf rule — the TBS hash of the vendor's own certificate; and
  • a publisher rule — the TBS hash of the certificate authority one level below the root, plus the vendor's common name.

The publisher rule is what makes this survive certificate renewal: when a vendor reissues its signing certificate under the same CA, the publisher rule still matches. The AnyDesk and ScreenConnect installers on the original test PC already prove that.

This is why renaming the file does not help an attacker, why saving it to Downloads does not help, and why running it from a USB stick does not help — none of those change the signature.

The policy carries a fixed policy ID ({2D13BFB7-4304-4847-9CDD-37820D3EE9B7}), so installing a newer build replaces the previous policy instead of stacking a second one. Both kits share that ID, so either kit replaces the other's install.

Full technical detail: docs/how-it-works.md.

Testing it

  1. Install the policy in audit mode (the Test mode button, or Run-RmmAppControl.bat -Mode Audit).
  2. Close the remote tool if it is already running — App Control blocks new process starts and does not kill running ones.
  3. Start the tool.
  4. Open Event Viewer → Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → CodeIntegrity → Operational and look for event 3076.
  5. Press BLOCK, close the tool, start it again — you should get event 3077 and the program should not run.

Note that these events carry the policy ID, not the policy name, which is why the status view filters on the GUID. More detail, including a safe way to trigger a policy check without actually running a tool, is in docs/testing.md.

Limits — read this before you rely on it

  • Unsigned tools are not covered. App Control here works by certificate, so an unsigned or self-signed remote tool gets through. The ESET "potentially unsafe applications" toggle is the backstop.
  • Windows Home is untested. App Control on Home editions is claimed by third parties but this project has not verified it. If you deploy to a Home PC, run audit mode first and confirm events appear.
  • The v.3 RustDesk block has not been observed on a PC yet. The rules were verified against the real RustDesk installer's certificate by inspection, and all 32 compiled policies were validated, but no live RustDesk block has been recorded. Test it in audit mode.
  • The window buttons have not been clicked by an automated test. Each window opens and was inspected, but the BLOCK/UNDO/Test buttons need administrator rights and were exercised by hand, not automatically. They call the same install script that was verified.
  • The ESET website paste is manual and a technician MUST do it by hand. ESET's URL list import is not scripted, and the tool cannot verify it happened. See The ESET paste and docs/eset-import-guide.md.
  • The ESET website list only covers HTTP/HTTPS, and HTTPS needs ESET's SSL/TLS filtering enabled. A tool that is already installed and connects over its own protocol may still connect.
  • Vendor certificates rotate. Rebuilding periodically from the upstream catalogue keeps the list current; the publisher rules cover most renewals.

The upstream data source is LOLRMM (https://lolrmm.io, repo magicsword-io/LOLRMM, Apache-2.0), a catalogue of around 358 RMM and remote-access tools including each one's code-signing certificates.

Configuration

Two deployment-specific values are named constants, near the top of their scripts. Change these (and nothing else) to brand the tool for your own shop:

Constant File Purpose
$PolicyName src/appcontrol/Build-RmmAppControl.v2026-10-11.3.ps1 Friendly name written into every generated policy
$LogDirName src/appcontrol/Install-RmmAppControl.v2026-10-11.3.ps1 Folder created under %ProgramData% for the log file

Do not change the policy GUID. PCs that already carry this policy are keyed to it; a different GUID would install a second policy alongside the first instead of replacing it. Changing it knowingly requires a migration step that removes the old policy — that is not automated here.

To change the default toggles (for example to block Splashtop out of the box), edit the default variant in Build-RmmAppControl and rebuild, or simply untick Splashtop in the window before pressing BLOCK and let it reinstall.

Rebuilding the policy and the release ZIPs

The pre-built policies in policy/ are committed, so ordinary use needs nothing else. Rebuild when you want to pick up new tools or refreshed certificates.

To rebuild the release ZIPs (both kits, with the 1\/2\ split asserted on the result):

./build/build-release.sh          # writes dist/*.zip + .sha256

Requires Windows 10/11 Pro or Enterprise (the ConfigCI module) and PowerShell 5.1:

# from the repo root, in an elevated PowerShell
.\src\appcontrol\Build-RmmAppControl.v2026-10-11.3.ps1
.\src\appcontrol\Build-RmmAppControl.v2026-10-11.3.ps1 -IncludeOptional        # add school/enterprise vendors
.\src\appcontrol\Build-RmmAppControl.v2026-10-11.3.ps1 -ExcludeSigner "Vendor Name"

Then install the result:

.\src\appcontrol\Run-RmmAppControl.bat -Mode Enforce -Variant T1A1S0R1
.\src\appcontrol\Run-RmmAppControl.bat -Mode Audit
.\src\appcontrol\Run-RmmAppControl.bat            # status (default)

Vendor names for -ExcludeSigner are the Publisher column in policy/signers.csv. PCs that cannot rebuild (a Home PC) just need the rebuilt policy/ folder copied next to them.

Safety

What this deliberately does not touch:

  • the kernel/driver signing scenario — only user-mode code is restricted;
  • script enforcement — PowerShell is not put into Constrained Language Mode;
  • any other App Control policy on the machine.

It is reversible: UNDO in the window, or

.\src\appcontrol\Run-RmmAppControl.bat -Mode Remove

then restart. That removes the policy this project installed and nothing else.

Repository layout

src/appcontrol/    Build- / Install- / Run-RmmAppControl   (ONE shared copy, used by both kits)
src/eset/          Get-LolrmmUrlList  (website list)  and Get-LolrmmHipsList  (experimental path list)
kits/1/            START-HERE.bat + window   (PROGRAM 1: the App Control program blocker)
kits/2/            START-HERE.bat + window   (PROGRAM 2: the ESET website list)
kits/windows-only/ START-HERE.bat + window (App Control only, one window)
revert/            Run-Revert.bat + Revert-RemoteAccessBlock (both variants) + Install-ESET-Revert
policy/            the prebuilt policies - 32 toggle combinations + signers.csv (generated output)
build/             build-release.sh - builds BOTH release ZIPs and asserts the 1\/2\ split on them
docs/              how-it-works, eset-import-guide, testing, CHANGELOG
archive/           the original ESET HIPS prototype, kept for history

The scripts resolve the folders relative to themselves, so the repo layout works in place and a built release ZIP (which lays the scripts out side by side) works standalone.

The revert tool follows the same rule in two ways: the kit resolves it either from revert\ (repo) or from the loose files beside the installer (release ZIP), and once installed on a PC it resolves everything — its own scripts, the guide and the policies — from C:\RemoteAccessToolBlocker\ alone.

Scripts deployed to other machines carry their version in the filename — Name.vYYYY-MM-DD.N.ps1. The .bat launchers auto-detect the newest with dir /b /o-n, so superseded versions can be removed once a new one works.

policy/ is generated output. It is committed because Windows Home PCs cannot build it themselves; it is rebuilt by Build-RmmAppControl.

Credits

  • LOLRMM (magicsword-io/LOLRMM, Apache-2.0) — the catalogue of remote-access tools and their code-signing certificates. The policies, the signer list and the ESET website lists in this repository are derived from its data. See NOTICE.
  • Microsoft — the AllowAll.xml example policy and the documented recommended-block-rules layout this policy is built on.
  • The RustDesk signing certificate is not in LOLRMM. It was taken from the official RustDesk Windows build and is embedded in the builder. See NOTICE.

Disclaimer

Provided as-is, without warranty of any kind. Test in audit mode first and confirm the events before you enforce, particularly on Windows Home and with RustDesk. Blocking a remote-access tool may cut off your own support access to that PC — check every toggle before you press BLOCK.

This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or supported by ESET, Microsoft, or any of the vendors named. All trademarks belong to their respective owners.

remote-diagnostics.html:
Remote Diagnostics

One window to find out why a Windows PC crashes, freezes, won't print or won't wake up.

When a PC misbehaves, the clues are scattered: event logs, crash dumps, driver versions, print queues, startup items, the network. Remote Diagnostics collects all of it in one run, decodes the useful parts (blue screens, GPU resets, failed resumes, stuck printers) and hands you a single zip file with a short REVIEW LIST of what to look at first. It can run on the PC itself or pull the same logs from another PC on the network.

Quick start

  1. Copy this whole folder onto the PC (USB stick, shared drive, remote session). Keep the files together.
  2. Double-click Run-RemoteDiagGui.bat and say Yes to the administrator prompt.
  3. Pick a tool card, set its options, press Run and watch the live output.
  4. When it finishes, click Open folder / Open zip location. Send the zip to whoever is helping.

Every tool also has its own Run-*.bat launcher if you prefer a plain console.

The tools

Cards marked READ-ONLY only look. Cards marked CHANGES THIS PC ask before they run, and the window can't be closed halfway through one.

Tool Launcher What it does
Pull logs from THIS PC Run-PullLocalLogs.bat Event logs, blue-screen decoding and minidumps, GPU/TDR resets, print-spooler errors and every print queue, network state (with a public IP / ISP check), startup items and scheduled tasks, EFI partition usage. One zip, with a REVIEW LIST on top. Default look-back 72 hours (1 to 168).
Pull logs from ANOTHER PC Run-PullRemoteLogs.bat The same pull over the network (WinRM) from a PC where Enable remote diagnostics was run. Needs a local admin account on that PC. The password goes straight to the script and is never shown, saved or logged.
Enable remote diagnostics Run-EnableRemoteDiag.bat Run on the PC you want to diagnose. Opens WinRM and remote event-log access, and turns itself off again after 48 hours.
Revert remote diagnostics now revert-remote-diag.ps1 Closes that access early.
Deep persistence inventory Run-PullPersistence.bat Everything that can start a program or script by itself (tasks, Run keys, services, WMI, every user's profile), with hashes and copies of suspicious scripts. Slow, and the output is sensitive.
EFI partition usage Run-CheckEspUsage.bat "EFI partition full"? Shows who filled it: Windows, the PC maker or firmware updates. Mounts it read-only and unmounts after.
Camera and startup check Run-CheckCameraAndStartup.bat Camera devices, drivers, privacy settings, USB power saving and startup items. The console launcher also offers fixes, asking for each one.
Watch a print freeze Run-WatchPrintFreeze.bat Start it, then print the job that freezes. It logs every change in the spooler, the app and the queues, and saves events and crash reports when you stop it.
Switch printer WSD -> TCP/IP Run-SwitchPrinterToTcpIp.bat The usual fix for a printer that stalls: moves the queue from a WSD port to a standard TCP/IP port at the printer's IP, keeps the queue name, restarts the spooler and clears stuck jobs. Has a -DryRun mode.

Two more, outside the window:

  • Run-CheckWakeDevices.bat: for devices that stop working after sleep or hibernate. Optional live sleep test (snapshot, sleep, wake, compare), plus every wake, failed resume and device error grouped by how often it happens right after waking. Report only; never changes anything.
  • Pull-BootFailureLogs.bat: for a PC that won't boot at all. Run it from the recovery Command Prompt (WinRE) or a WinPE USB. Pure batch, no PowerShell needed. Collects Startup Repair logs, the boot log, CBS/DISM and setup logs, offline event logs, BCD and disk layout onto the USB stick, and turns boot logging on for the next attempt. Set the PE_DRIVE letter at the top first.

What leaves the PC?

  • The output stays on the PC: on the Desktop of the person who is signed in (RemoteDiagLogs\), or the folder you choose. Nothing is uploaded.
  • One online lookup: the pull tools ask ip-api.com for the PC's public IP and internet provider, so the report can flag content-filtering ISPs that interfere with certificates and updates.
  • Logs can contain computer names, user names and installed software. Treat the zip as private.

Requirements

  • Windows 10 or 11, Windows PowerShell 5.1 (built in). Run as administrator; the .bat files ask for you.
  • For pulling from another PC: both PCs on the same network, TCP 5985 open, and Enable remote diagnostics run on the target first.

For developers

  • The window (gui\) is a front end only. It runs the same dated scripts the Run-*.bat files run, with the same arguments, and shows their output. Design notes: docs/gui-architecture.md.
  • Each script carries its version in its file name (<Name>.v<YYYY-MM-DD>.<N>.ps1). The launchers pick the newest one automatically.
  • Tests: from a non-elevated Windows PowerShell, run each tests\gui\Test-*.ps1.
  • New-SelfContainedBat.ps1 wraps any script into a single self-elevating .bat for locked-down PCs where Group Policy blocks .ps1 files.

License

MIT. Made by Rubin IT, with pupontech. Use it at your own risk.

student-times.html:
Student Times

Set the hours a Windows account is allowed to sign in, with a point-and-click grid.

Schools and homes often need student or kids' computers to be usable only at certain times. Windows can already do this (net user <name> /times:...), but typing those commands by hand is slow and easy to get wrong. Student Times puts a simple weekly grid on top of it: click the hours that are allowed, press one button, done. It also handles the extras that make the restriction actually stick: logging the student out when time is up, stopping them from changing the clock, and pushing the same schedule to every PC in a classroom.

Quick start

  1. Copy this whole folder onto the student PC (or run it from a USB stick or a shared drive). Keep the files together.
  2. Double-click Run-StudentTimes.bat and say Yes to the administrator prompt.
  3. Type the Windows account name (for example students), or click Accounts on this PC... and tick the accounts you want.
  4. Click or drag across the grid: green = allowed, grey = blocked.
  5. Tick Run it immediately here and click Generate. That's it: the account can now sign in only during the green hours.

No installation and no PowerShell settings to change first. Works on Windows 10 and 11 with the built-in Windows PowerShell 5.1.

What's in the window

Daily Use

  • The weekly grid. 7 days x 24 hours. Click or drag to toggle. Copy / Paste buttons copy a whole day onto another.
  • Load Current Schedule From This PC reads what the account is set to right now.
  • Generate + Copy Command makes the exact net user command and copies it, if you prefer to paste it into an administrator Command Prompt yourself. Tick Run it immediately here to have the tool apply it for you (it asks first).
  • Several accounts at once. Accounts on this PC... lists the local accounts with tick boxes (common student account names are pre-ticked, administrators never are). Every action then applies to all ticked accounts.
  • Temporary unlock. Unlock Today / 2 Days / 3 Days opens the account right away and locks it again by itself at midnight of the last day, putting the saved schedule back. Re-lock Now ends the unlock early.
  • Quick slots. Save up to three named schedules (e.g. "Term", "Holidays") and load one in a click.
  • Schedule a change for later. Pick a date and time and the grid is applied then by Task Scheduler, even if nobody is signed in.

Setup / Verify (once per PC)

  • Logout tasks. Windows' logon hours stop a new sign-in, but they don't throw out someone who is already signed in. Student Times creates scheduled tasks that lock or sign out the account at the end of each allowed block. They are kept in step with the grid automatically.
  • Time-change rights. Removes the right to change the clock or time zone, so a student can't just move the clock back.
  • Check / Fix Time Settings. Makes sure the PC's clock really syncs (with a list of backup time servers), keeps daylight-saving on and the time zone fixed.
  • Auto-lock new accounts. Optional. Any new non-admin account created later gets the same hours automatically.
  • Verify Everything prints a plain report of what is set and what is missing.

Network Push (a whole classroom at once)

  1. On every PC in the group, run Enable-PushAcceptance.bat once as administrator (or click Enable This PC To Receive Pushes). This turns on Windows Remote Management (WinRM) for the local network.
  2. On any one PC, click Scan Network For PCs. PCs that are ready are ticked for you.
  3. Enter a shared local administrator account, then Test Ticked PCs (changes nothing) and Push Current Grid To Ticked PCs.

To copy a newer version of this tool onto all the student PCs, run Update-StudentTimesGui.bat 192.168.1.21 192.168.1.22 ... (PC names or IPs).

Desktop Lock

  • Stops the student account from changing the background, theme and colours, and turns off Windows Spotlight (the rotating lock-screen pictures, tips and promoted apps).
  • Optionally sets one fixed lock-screen / sign-in picture for the whole PC that nobody can change.
  • Undo removes every setting it added.

Good to know

  • Run it as administrator. It changes local account policy, so it needs admin rights. The .bat asks for them for you.
  • Logs stay on the PC. Each change is logged next to the script (StudentTimesLog.csv) so you can see what was set and when. Nothing is sent anywhere.
  • Hour steps only. Windows stores logon hours as whole hours, so 15:30 cut-offs are not possible with this mechanism.
  • Daylight saving. Windows stores logon hours in standard time. After a clock change, check on one PC that the first lock-out happens at the right time.
  • Network Push needs the PCs to reach each other on TCP port 5985 (WinRM) on the same local network.
  • If double-clicking the .bat does nothing, PowerShell may be locked down by Group Policy. Open PowerShell as administrator and run powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File ".\Set-StudentTimes.v2026-11-23.1.ps1".

Files

File What it is
Run-StudentTimes.bat Start here. Asks for admin rights and opens the window.
Set-StudentTimes.v<date>.ps1 The tool itself. The date in the name is the version.
Enable-PushAcceptance.bat / .ps1 One-time setup so a PC can receive a Network Push.
Update-StudentTimesGui.bat / .ps1 Copies this folder to other PCs over the network.

License

MIT. Made by Rubin IT for the schools we look after, shared in case it helps yours. Use it at your own risk and test on one PC before rolling out to a whole lab.
